terminal.description: A shell in your workspace where the demo fetches passenger lists from a busy fake harbour server, retries, and cancels one request part way through.

tasks.title: Retry with backoff
tasks.description:
Implement `retry(task, options)` in `src/retry.js`. It calls `task({ attempt, signal })` until it resolves, and resolves with its value. `options` is `{ attempts = 4, baseMs = 100, signal, sleep }`.

- `attempt` counts from 1
- if the error's `retryable` property is not `true`, reject with it at once
- if it is retryable and attempts are left, `await sleep(baseMs * 2 ** (attempt - 1), { signal })` and try again, so the waits are 100, 200, 400 ms by default
- after the last attempt fails, reject with that last error, without a final wait

For this task `signal` can stay unused; the third task adds it.

**Timing:** `sleep` is an option that defaults to `sleep` from `src/sleep.js`. The check passes a fake sleep that records every delay you ask for and returns at once, so no real time passes.
nextSteps: Run `node src/demo.js` and read the first block.
Write a loop that calls the task and returns its value when it works.
Decide in the catch whether to give up or wait and go round again.
Run the demo: S1 should succeed on call 3 and X9 fail on call 1.
hints: There are three ways out of each attempt: success, a failure worth retrying, and a failure that is not.
A `for` loop over `attempt` with a `try` and `catch` inside reads well. The `return` inside the `try` ends the whole function.
In the catch, rethrow when the error is not retryable or when `attempt` has reached `attempts`. Sleep after the catch, before the next turn.

tasks.title: A sleep you can cancel
tasks.description:
`sleep(ms, options)` in `src/sleep.js` works, but nothing can stop it. Make it cancellable. `options` is `{ signal, setTimeout, clearTimeout }`.

- start one timer with `setTimeout(callback, ms)` and resolve when it fires
- if `signal` is already aborted, reject with `signal.reason` and start no timer
- if `signal` aborts while waiting, clear the timer and reject with `signal.reason`
- once the timer has fired, remove the abort listener you added
- without a `signal` it simply waits

**Timing:** `setTimeout` and `clearTimeout` are options that default to the real ones. The check passes a fake clock that records the delay, fires the timer by hand and notes whether you cleared it. It also counts the abort listeners left on the signal.
nextSteps: Handle a signal that is already aborted.
Start the timer and keep its id.
Listen for the abort event and clean up in both directions.
Run the checks and read which case fails, if any.
hints: An `AbortSignal` has an `aborted` flag, a `reason`, and fires an `abort` event. You need all three.
Two things can happen first: the timer fires or the signal aborts. Whichever comes first should undo the other.
Name the abort handler so you can pass the same function to `removeEventListener` inside the timer callback, and call `clearTimeout(timer)` inside the handler.

tasks.title: Stop when asked
tasks.description:
Teach `retry` in `src/retry.js` to stop when `options.signal` (an `AbortSignal`, possibly missing) aborts, so no retry or timer runs after that.

- pass the signal on: `task({ attempt, signal })` and `sleep(ms, { signal })`
- if the signal is already aborted, reject with `signal.reason` without calling `task`
- once the signal has aborted, start no new attempt and no new sleep, and reject with `signal.reason`
- this holds even if the attempt in progress then fails with a retryable error, or a sleep finishes anyway
- everything from the first task still works without a signal

**Timing:** `sleep` is an option. The check passes a fake sleep that it finishes by hand, and that rejects on abort like the real one, except in one case where it ignores the signal on purpose.
nextSteps: Pass the signal to the task and to sleep.
Find every point where your loop is about to start something new.
Check the signal at each of them.
Run the demo: S2 should stop at about 120 ms with no calls after it.
hints: Aborting cannot reach inside a promise that is already running. Your code has to look at the signal whenever it gets control back.
`signal?.throwIfAborted()` throws `signal.reason` when the signal is aborted and does nothing otherwise, including when there is no signal.
Check at the top of each turn of the loop (covers the start and after waking) and first thing in the catch (covers a failure that arrives after an abort).
